There’s no debate who the prize of the offseason is for the New York Mets. Tarik Skubal is the top target for a team in need of an ace with an owner whose wallet is wide open. If the Mets do nothing but sign Skubal and fill in gaps with some minor caulking, you’ll see their projected win total go up.
The Mets do need to plan for life without Skubal like they did last offseason when Edwin Diaz fled to the Los Angeles Dodgers and Kyle Tucker ended up signing with them, too. Their pivots, Luke Weaver and Bo Bichette, ended up having more productive years.
Pivots for the Mets won’t just include other starting pitchers. Stacking the bullpen, finding a bat, etc. are other ways to fix any Skubal diss. As a representative of two ball clubs in 2026, Skubal got to call himself teammates with a bunch of different dudes. There are two players he teamed up with for the Mets to prioritize this offseason and another pair to stay far away from.
A pair of Tarik Skubal teammates in 2026 the Mets should go after and another duo to avoid entirely
The Mets should target Evan Phillips
Evan Phillips might quietly be one of the best matches for the Mets in free agency. The 32-year-old righty has already excelled in the big Los Angeles market. Experienced as a closer and setup man, his 10.3 K/9 rate along with 2.4 BB/9 as a member of the Dodgers makes him an appealing option to take on the role vacated when the Mets traded Luke Weaver. Some additional Devin Williams insurance is a must. Phillips, as a right-handed line of defense, feels worth a heavy pursuit. What’s more, he has tossed 18.1 scoreless postseason innings. The Mets have to get there first for that to matter. Phillips can certainly help.
The Mets should stay away from Kris Bubic
Kris Bubic might be one of those pitchers about to blossom in his late 20s. Let him do it somewhere else. Health has been a major issue for him. He combined to pitch 55 innings for the Kansas City Royals and Dodgers this past year. Bubic was a rumored trade target for the Mets last offseason prior to landing Freddy Peralta. As skilled as he is, the ability to have availability should have the Mets refusing to even consider him.
The Mets should target Alex Vesia
If the Mets feel they need to spend on a lefty reliever, they could do far worse than Alex Vesia. In fact, they might not be able to do much better. A lot of those same pros mentioned for Phillips apply here. As laid back as California is, you don’t get a free pass playing sports in Hollywood. Vesia has pitched 50 or more games every year since 2022 and in his career owns a 12 K/9 rate. He owns a 1.59 ERA in the playoffs. He’d be a perfect alternative to Adrian Morejon who could be getting a qualifying offer.
The Mets should stay away from Casey Mize
Sorry, but not. Don’t even think about Casey Mize. A lifetime 4.22 ERA and a disappointing finish with the San Diego Padres after a career-year started off with the Tigers erases any thought of making Mize one of two starters the Mets could target. He definitely wouldn’t be the singular addition. Mize doesn’t strike out enough batters nor is he a heavy ground ball pitcher. This offseason isn’t the time to add guys who might need adjustments. The Mets need a surer thing and Mize ain’t it.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are entering a transitionary period this offseason, with a list of nine potential free agents that includes Alex Vesia among them.
Facing an uncertain future, the left-handed reliever took to Instagram to thank his teammates and fans for their support this season and over the past six years.
Vesia improved upon his 2025 season despite a regression in WHIP, walk rate and strikeout rate. He accomplished this thanks to a lower batting average against and cutting his home runs allowed by over half. That all came while attempting to move past personal tragedy for his family.
The 30-year-old was an important contributor to a Dodgers bullpen that finished in the top five in ERA.
He became one of L.A.’s most trusted relievers since joining the organization in 2021. Vesia has finished with a 2.64 ERA or lower in four of his six seasons with the Dodgers and posted a 2.87 ERA overall during that span.
A reunion makes sense for both sides, but is complicated by the future of the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and the current state of the Dodgers’ roster.
The current CBA expires at 9 p.m. PT on Dec. 1. Players can sign new contracts prior to that point, but will be prohibited from doing so during an expected lockout that will likely drag well into 2027.
As for the Dodgers’ chances of re-signing Vesia, it could depend heavily on how his market develops. The organization is not likely to add another expensive bullpen contract with so much money invested in the group already.
An additional factor working against a reunion is how adept the front office is at identifying reliever talent. The Dodgers can allocate resources elsewhere if they can find a cheaper alternative.
Kiké Hernández’s posts potential goodbye to Dodgers fans
News of Miguel Rojas’ retirement leaves the Dodgers with eight decisions to make regarding potential free agents, one of which is Kiké Hernández.
Like Vesia, Hernández also took to social media to reflect on his time with the Dodgers.
The 35-year-old was open about his wish to re-sign with L.A. once again, but the chances of a deal materializing is not guaranteed.
The Dodgers’ other free agents this offseason include Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Tarik Skubal, and Blake Treinen.

MILWAUKEE, WI — Dave Roberts gave Milwaukee credit for the work that put the Dodgers in a two-game hole. After Monday’s 7–4 loss, he pointed to the Brewers’ longer at-bats, contact and ability to create trouble on the bases. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s early exit forced Roberts to cover more than six innings with his bullpen, and two leads slipped away. With the series heading to Los Angeles, Roberts wants length from Blake Snell and more help from the lineup.
A rare rough outing for Yamamoto
Roberts saw Yamamoto struggle to find his usual sharpness, with the third inning pushing his pitch count toward an early exit.
“He wasn’t sharp today,” Roberts said. “You can see from that Contreras at-bat in the third inning that really stressed him. You’ve got to give him a lot of credit. Then you follow that up with the Bauers at-bat, and the pitch count certainly crept up.”
“At that point, you’ve got Yelich, call it 70 pitches, and you’re trying to think about maybe getting him through it, as one of your guys, to shorten the game and give us a little bit of length.”
Yelich’s two-run single ended Yamamoto’s afternoon after 2⅔ innings.
“Once Yelich gets a hit, we’ve got to find a way to put it out and give ourselves a chance,” Roberts said. “He just didn’t have it tonight, which is very rare.”
Asked about close pitches to Brice Turang that went unchallenged, Roberts explained why those calls rest with the players.
“Will’s got a great view back there, as all catchers do,” he said. “As an offense, you try to defer to the hitter to save those challenges, defer to the catcher to save those challenges. In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike.”
“If you look back and that’s a called third strike, he doesn’t double, and that changes the outing. But I’m not back there. You’ve got to trust the players to make those decisions when they get in those spots.”
Why Sasaki pitched one inning
Roki Sasaki worked a scoreless fourth before Roberts turned to Kris Bubic in the fifth. Roberts said the run of left-handed hitters made that a spot he wanted for Bubic.
“You’re trying to cover six-plus innings,” he said. “I felt Bubic, you get four out of five left-handed hitters, and that’s a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren’t going to hit for them.”
“You’ve got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy where, in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic. He tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras, and then he hits a homer.”
“That’s a decision I made. That’s his lane, to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
Contreras’ homer tied the game. In the sixth, Roberts stayed with Brock Stewart to face him, hoping for a ground ball with runners at first and third.
“I felt like we had a chance to put him on the ground, get a double-play ball,” Roberts said. “Contreras didn’t hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that’s what they do.”
Milwaukee creates the trouble
The Brewers finished with 12 hits to the Dodgers’ three. Roberts felt the gap began with how the teams handled their at-bats.
“They saw a ton more pitches than we did. And they had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom,” he said. “They put the ball in play, created havoc. That’s the difference in the game.”
Asked about the Dodgers’ struggles against Milwaukee’s bullpen, Roberts included the starter in his assessment.
“We had three hits tonight. It was some of the starter, some of the bullpen,” he said. “They’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re finding ways to win pitches better than we are.”
“Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit. There were a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
Snell gets the next chance
Roberts wants Snell to give the Dodgers a longer start in Game 3, allowing the bullpen to work with a lead.
“We need Snell to go out there and give us some length, give us a typical Blake Snell outing,” he said. “I know Blake has a bad taste in his mouth from that last outing against the Braves. You’re going to see a locked-in, focused Snell.”
“On the other side of things, we’ve got to support him offensively, too.”
Roberts still sees a path back into the series, starting with one win at home.
“If you look at Game 3, I like where we’re at as far as who’s pitching, where our bullpen is at, being at home,” he said. “Then you’ve got to go from there.”
“Can we do it? Absolutely. You want to get that first one.”

LOS ANGELES, CA—While the 2026 Major League Baseball postseason remains in play, the offseason has officially begun for the Los Angeles Dodgers after their anticlimactic series sweep at the hands of the National League champion Milwaukee Brewers.
After the conclusion of the 2026 Fall Classic, the Dodgers are set to have a total of nine free agents hit the open market, an increase from five last season.
While the list reads as nine, it is essentially eight, as veteran infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball after the Dodgers’ Game Four loss.
Free Agents
(9): Blake Treinen, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Alex Vesia, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Tarik Skubal
Blake Treinen
Veteran right-hander Blake Treinen’s season ended during the final week of September after a right shoulder setback that forced him off the Dodgers postseason roster.
Treinen returned to Los Angeles after his 2024 World Series heroics on a 2-year, $14 million contract, and now the 38-year-old will be without a home entering an offseason that may be the final season of his career.
Evan Phillips
Right-hander Evan Phillips missed all of 2025 and returned toward the middle of the 2026 regular season due to Tommy John surgery. However, in his games played, he was very effective, going 3-2 with a 3.46 ERA.
Still, Phillips will be entering his age 33 season and has already missed significant time due to right elbow/arm injuries, and with multiple pitchers in the pipeline, it’s not hard to see the Dodgers moving on.
Kris Bubic
Acquired at the trade deadline, left-hander Kris Bubic is likely to get a contract this Winter as a starter, since that was his primary role before injuries derailed his 2026 season.
Bubic was an All-Star in 2025 and, with a thin free-agent market, could land a nice contract from a team desperate for starting pitching.
Miguel Rojas
Shortly after the conclusion of Game Four of the NLCS, veteran utility infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement from Major League Baseball, bringing an end to his 13-year playing career.
Rojas is expected to remain with the Dodgers organization in a player devleopment/coaching role.
Kiké Hernández
October hero Kiké Hernández is hitting free agency yet again this Winter, and after a subpar performance in October, minus one huge home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS, not much is known about whether the Dodgers will try to run it back for another 1-year deal.
Overall, Hernández missed most of the season while recovering from elbow surgery and an oblique injury and hit 4 home runs in 90 at-bats while posting a below-average 82 OPS+.
The fan favorite will enter his age-36 season, likely ending his Dodgers tenure for the second time.
Alex Vesia
Arguably the biggest free agent from the Dodgers bullpen this Winter is left-hander Alex Vesia, who has likely pitched his way to a sizable multi-year contract that the Dodgers might not be inclined to match.
Vesia, 30, posted an elite 2.64 ERA and struck out 74 batters despite a below-average fastball velocity, but with backend pitching at a premium, his market is likely to be heavy.
Brusdar Graterol
Brusdar Graterol’s career has been defined by injuries, and that likely will force his time in Dodger Blue to come to an end this Winter.
Despite a 2.78 career ERA, the right-hander has pitched only 7.1 innings for the Dodgers since the 2024 regular season, missing the entire 2025 and 2026 seasons due to right shoulder surgery.
Eric Lauer
Like Bubic, left-hander Eric Lauer will enter the market as a starting pitcher, and after a second-half renaissance with the Dodgers, where he went 7-2 with a 4.50 ERA, he could be a dependable backend starter to eat innings for a variety of clubs.
Tarik Skubal
The consensus No. 1 free agent this Winter across baseball is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is set to demand a massive multi-year contract that could go north of $400 million.
While the Dodgers will no doubt be involved, it’s hard to imagine them matching that while already having so many long-term deals tied up, especially in their starting rotation already.
Skubal is likely to sign before the MLB lockout on December 1st to maximize his contract, such as fellow Scott Boras client Corey Seager did after the 2021 season.

LOS ÁNGELES - La temporada baja ha llegado antes de lo previsto para los Dodgers.
Antes de haber asimilado por completo la derrota del jueves por la noche (6-4) ante los Cerveceros en el Juego 4 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional —resultado que puso fin a su temporada y a su intento de lograr un tercer título consecutivo—, los Dodgers tuvieron que afrontar la realidad de que probablemente se avecinan cambios en el equipo.
Los Dodgers perderán a nueve jugadores debido a la agencia libre, un grupo encabezado por la figura más destacada del mercado, Tarik Skubal. Los otros jugadores que pronto serán agentes libres son el venezolano Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen, Eric Lauer, Kris Bubic y el venezolano Brusdar Graterol.
Gran parte del núcleo del equipo de Los Ángeles permanecerá intacto en el futuro previsible, por lo que la ventana competitiva no se está cerrando; sin embargo, este podría ser un periodo de transición entre una era del béisbol de los Dodgers y otra.
"Nunca puedes pensar que este es el final", dijo Rojas, quien permanecerá en la organización desempeñando un papel en el desarrollo de jugadores. "Y conozco muy bien a esta organización; no se conformarán con esta derrota".
A lo largo de 14 participaciones consecutivas en la postemporada, los Dodgers han encontrado formas fluidas de incorporar talento joven a sus plantillas para complementar a su núcleo de veteranos experimentados. Ese proceso ya ha comenzado con el dominicano Josue De Paula —el prospecto número 4 a nivel general según MLB Pipeline—, así como con el receptor suplente Dalton Rushing y el jugador de cuadro Alex Freeland.
No obstante, es posible que los Dodgers deban adoptar un enfoque más deliberado para asignar roles más destacados a sus jugadores jóvenes de cara al futuro, lo que dará lugar a decisiones interesantes durante esta temporada baja.
"No conocemos el futuro", comentó el dominicano Teóscar Hernández. "Pero algo que sabemos es que nos preocupamos los unos por los otros, nos cuidamos mutuamente y nos apoyamos durante todo el año... Este grupo es realmente especial, no por lo que hemos logrado en los últimos dos años y en este, sino simplemente por la unión que tenemos".
A continuación, un vistazo a algunas de las decisiones más importantes sobre el roster que deberán tomar los Dodgers durante esta temporada baja:
¿Participarán en la puja por Skubal?
Los Dodgers se desprendieron de dos prospectos clasificados entre los 100 mejores —el abridor listo para las Grandes Ligas River Ryan y el jardinero Zyhir Hope—, además del lanzador derecho Brady Smith, a cambio de contar con Skubal por un periodo de hasta tres meses. No fueron el único equipo dispuesto a hacer una gran inversión por un talento del calibre de Skubal, y lo mismo ocurrirá cuando este llegue al mercado de agentes libres por primera vez.
Skubal ganó su caso de arbitraje salarial contra los Tigres la temporada baja pasada, obteniendo un salario récord de US$32 millones. Se espera ampliamente que consiga la mayor cantidad de dinero garantizado jamás otorgada a un lanzador en la agencia libre, superando el contrato de 12 años y US$325 millones de Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
En su año previo a la agencia libre, Skubal se perdió seis semanas tras someterse a una cirugía en el codo izquierdo, pero aun así completó otra campaña sólida, registrando una marca de 12-7 y una efectividad de 2.72 en 26 aperturas con los Tigres y los Dodgers. Prefirió no hablar sobre su futuro inmediatamente después de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional (SCLN).
"Sí, realmente no voy a hacer comentarios sobre mi futuro", dijo Skubal. "El día de hoy es una porquería, ya sabes, y en eso es en lo que estoy pensando ahora mismo".
Aun así, Skubal expresó su agradecimiento por el tiempo que pasó con los Dodgers.
"Una organización increíble, compañeros increíbles, una afición increíble", dijo. "Es un honor llevar las letras 'L.A.' en el pecho y en la gorra".
¿Cómo le darán tiempo de juego para De Paula?
En septiembre, De Paula hizo que el salto de Doble-A a las Grandes Ligas pareciera sencillo, impresionando tanto a los Dodgers que logró entrar en el roster de postemporada como opción de bateador emergente. Sin embargo, su limitación radicaba en que el equipo de Grandes Ligas lo veía únicamente como bateador designado, una posición ocupada por Shohei Ohtani.
"Creo que la mejora que Josue mostró en los jardines entre 2025 y 2026 es real", comentó el mes pasado Andrew Friedman, presidente de operaciones de béisbol. "Y para nosotros, se trata de dar otro gran paso de cara a 2027. Él tiene las herramientas y la capacidad para lograrlo".
Con el tiempo, los Dodgers tendrán que poner a De Paula a jugar en los jardines. No obstante, sus jardineros titulares —Teóscar Hernández, el cubano Andy Pages y Kyle Tucker— tienen contrato vigente hasta la próxima temporada.
Si los Dodgers consideran que De Paula está listo para ser jugador titular habitual, eso probablemente implicaría, como mínimo, limitar el tiempo de juego de Hernández. También podría darse una medida más drástica: buscar un equipo interesado en asumir la última temporada garantizada de su contrato de tres años y US$66 millones.
Otra opción sería que De Paula comenzara la temporada en Triple-A, donde podría trabajar en su defensa en un entorno de menor presión.
¿Qué jugadores veteranos clave regresarán?
Entre los agentes libres inminentes, algunas de las bajas más significativas en cuanto a liderazgo serían Kiké Hernández, Phillips, Vesia y Treinen. El bullpen ciertamente podría tener hueco para lanzadores de situaciones críticas como Phillips y Vesia, pero el encaje de Hernández entre los jugadores de posición no está tan claro.
Hernández, el propio "Mr. October" de los Dodgers, tuvo una temporada regular marcada por las lesiones. Tampoco estuvo a la altura de su habitual rendimiento en postemporada, conectando apenas un jonrón solitario en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional (SDLN) como único imparable. Es una figura importante en el vestuario y, aunque le encantaría volver a Los Ángeles, sabe que sus necesidades y las del equipo deben coincidir durante la agencia libre.
"Me encantaría intentarlo una vez más, tratar de ganar otro", dijo Hernández. "Pero realmente no sé qué va a pasar. Espero volver y, si no es así, espero poder jugar en un equipo ganador".

LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. They loaded up after winning their second straight title, signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in free agency and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. All they had to do was get through a Milwaukee Brewers team they swept in last year's NLCS in order to appear in a World Series against either Tampa Bay or Cleveland, both of whom L.A. would be favored to take care of.
Instead, the Dodgers' incredible run was stymied by Milwaukee in an NLCS that can only be classified as embarrassing for L.A. The Dodgers could not get anything going offensively, and their vaunted rotation underwhelmed. Now, with their three-peat bid having been a failure, an important offseason is ahead. Will Tarik Skubal be back? That shouldn't be ruled out. These other players, though, almost certainly won't be back with the Dodgers seeking revenge in 2027 (if there even is a 2027 season).
INF Miguel Rojas
Why not start out with an easy one? Miguel Rojas has made it clear that he plans on retiring after the 2026 campaign. He can always change his mind, and he told Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times that he wouldn't play for another team, but with Rojas now 37 years old and with a pair of World Series wins on his resume, what more does he have to play for?
Rojas retiring would be a tough blow for the Dodgers, given the fact that he's still a solid bench piece, is an important clubhouse presence, and recorded one of the biggest and unlikeliest hits in MLB history when he tied Game 7 of the 2025 World Series with a home run, but it's hard to imagine Rojas sticking around for another year.
RHP Blake Treinen
Once upon a time, Blake Treinen was one of the best relievers in the sport. He saved 38 games for the Athletics in 2018, and had a pair of sub-2.00 ERA seasons for the Dodgers in 2021 and 2024. Unfortunately, Treinen has a 4.47 ERA in 68 appearances since the start of the 2025 campaign, and injuries have limited him to fewer than 40 outings in each of those years.
Treinen missed nearly three months of the 2026 campaign with elbow inflammation, didn't pitch all that great upon his return, and was placed on the IL with shoulder inflammation at the end of the regular season. Injuries have been a common theme for Treinen over the course of his career, and while he had always been good enough to keep around despite his missed time, now, at 38 years old, he isn't what he once was. It's hard to envision the Dodgers being eager to bring him back.
LHP Kris Bubic
The Dodgers bolstered their pitching depth by acquiring Kris Bubic at the trade deadline from the Kansas City Royals. Sure, Bubic was hurt at the time, which made the move a bit risky, but L.A. made this move with the postseason in mind. Well, while Bubic came through with five scoreless appearances in the regular season, he allowed a run in each of his postseason appearances, taking a loss in the NLDS against the Braves and blowing a rare lead the Dodgers had in Game 2 of the NLCS against the Brewers.
These rough outings aren't reason enough to not want to bring Bubic back, but odds are, the southpaw is going to want to start (he was rock-solid in that role with the Royals), and I'm not sold that the Dodgers will be eager to guarantee him a rotation spot, with Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow locked in if healthy, and guys like Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan still in the organization. Odds are, Bubic will earn a solidified rotation spot elsewhere.
LHP Eric Lauer
The Dodgers dealt with a slew of pitching injuries, and brought Eric Lauer in to give them needed depth. To his credit, Lauer pitched quite well in his 13 appearances (11 starts) for the Dodgers. In fact, He allowed three earned runs or fewer in nine of his 11 starts and allowed just one run in eight innings in two appearances as a bulk reliever. If it weren't for a couple of especially brutal starts, Lauer's numbers in L.A. would've wound up looking much better than they did.
With that being said, Lauer ended the year on the IL with left elbow inflammation and, as is the case with Bubic, is probably looking for more of a solidified role than the Dodgers would be willing to give him. He'd be a solid option to bring back in a swingman role, but it's likely that the 31-year-old will end up elsewhere.
OF Teoscar Hernandez
Here's the big one. Teoscar Hernandez is the only player on this list under contract for 2027, and he's been a staple in L.A. since the 2024 campaign. There're a couple of reasons why it makes sense to move him, though. First, he's simply not worth the $17 million he's owed in 2027 after the year he just had. He still mashes left-handed pitching, but he had a subpar .695 OPS against righties in the regular season and is a very poor defensive outfielder. It's hard to justify playing him regularly on a team trying to contend.
Second, and perhaps most importantly, the Dodgers need to find a spot for top prospect Josue De Paula to play regularly. The ideal spot for De Paula, an outstanding hitter whose defense leaves much to be desired, would be DH, but that's Shohei Ohtani's spot for the foreseeable future. Kyle Tucker is locked into right field given his absurd contract, and De Paula can't play center field (nor should the Dodgers be eager to move off of Andy Pages). That leaves left field, Hernandez's spot, as the position where De Paula seems likeliest to slot in.
The Dodgers can keep Hernandez around as a platoon partner for De Paula, but a trade could make sense. Hernandez was in rumors last offseason, and I wouldn't be surprised to see those resurface this winter.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are two games away from being eliminated at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
With right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto having pitched in Game 2, the current state of affairs is far from where fans expected the Dodgers to be as the series heads back to LA. The 2025 World Series MVP lasted just 2.2 innings on Monday in an uncharacteristic one-strikeout performance, but there was still tons of baseball to be played after his exit.
After left-hander Alex Vesia finished off the third inning with four pitches, one of last year's October standouts in Roki Sasaki trotted out to the mound to face the Brewers in the fourth.
Sasaki's October success last season, especially in multi-inning spots, is partially why manager Dave Roberts was in a position to explain himself for only having Sasaki out to throw one frame.
The man who opened up the bottom of the fifth inning for LA, southpaw Kris Bubic, recorded just two outs on 22 pitches, one of which was turned into a solo home run for Brewers catcher William Contreras to tie the game.
Despite Sasaki's resume, Roberts went with the left-hander, but revealed he was looking for far more than two outs from the former All-Star.
"To me, you're trying to cover six-plus innings," Roberts said. "For me, I felt Bubic had four out of five left-handed hitters, and that's a perfect spot for him. I knew they weren't going to for him, and you got Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you've got a great spot for Bubic. Tries to go with the fastball up to Contreras and then hits a homer.
"That's a decision I made, and we just didn't — again, that's his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero."
After Bubic walked a batter to leave a man on first and second, Brock Stewart came in to end the inning. Instead of a fresh arm coming in for the bottom of the sixth, Stewart remained in the game. Three batters later, Contreras was back up to bat with a tie game, two on and one out.
Contreras hit the first pitch he saw 76.9 mph into the outfield grass to give his team the lead and Stewart was removed from the contest. Tanner Scott entered the game after him and promptly struck out the next two batters to get out of the inning.
Roberts was asked about why Stewart was in instead of Scott entering against an already hot Contreras.
"It just felt like trying to put Contreras on the ground," Roberts said. "Contreras didn't hit the ball hard. He flared it out to left field, drove in a run, and that's what they do."
Roberts continued to point out the differences between the kind of at-bats that the Brewers' brand is a byproduct of.
"I think for me just in total they saw a ton more pitches than we did," Roberts said. "They had much better at-bats than we did across the board top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc, and that's what they do, and we didn't do that.
"That's the difference in the game. I think that there's certainly a lot to unpack, but they did what needed to do tonight."

- Click here to listen to this article
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted just 2⅔ innings, and the Dodgers couldn’t hold multiple leads in a 7-4 loss to Milwaukee in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
- The Brewers’ relievers shut down Los Angeles for the second straight game, putting the Dodgers in a 2-0 series hole as the NLCS shifts to Dodger Stadium.
MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto stood on the same mound where just a year ago he’d thrown a complete game and was pummeled by Brewers fans’ chants:
“Yel-li! Yel-li!”
This time, en route to the Dodgers’ 7-4 loss to Milwaukee on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, Yamamoto had lasted only 2⅔ innings.
As American Family Field celebrated Brewers captain Christian Yelich’s two-run single for an early lead, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts emerged from the visiting dugout, ready to take the ball from the starter who’d made himself a household name with his postseason heroics.
Dodgers hitters are stymied by the Brewers bullpen, which throws five perfect innings in a 7-4 win that gives Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in the NLCS.
Yamamoto’s early exit put the onus on the Dodgers’ bullpen in a back-and-forth contest. And the Brewers’ bullpen shut down the Dodgers’ offense for the second straight game, pitching five hitless innings. The Dodgers finished with just three hits.
The NLCS heads to Los Angeles with the Brewers leading 2-0 in the best-of-seven series. The Dodgers will have home-field advantage for the next three games, needing to win four of the next five to return to the World Series.
It was the second straight highly touted pitching matchup, pitting Yamamoto against Logan Henderson, the Brewers’ 24-year-old budding star.
Yamamoto exited after giving up three runs and four hits in the shortest start of his career. Against Henderson, the Dodgers took advantage of mistakes by the Brewers’ usually fundamentally sound defense to score four runs against him, only two of which were earned.
The Dodgers’ offense started to chip away at Henderson right away. Leadoff hitter Mookie Betts worked a walk, which included a successful ABS challenge that turned a strikeout into a full count.
Betts then advanced to second on Freddie Freeman’s groundout to second and to third on a wild pitch.
The night before, Teoscar Hernández had zeroed in on the Dodgers’ at-bats with runners in scoring position in his postgame comments.
“We did a pretty good job,” he said after the Dodgers’ 2-1 loss in Game 1. “We just didn’t get the job done when we needed with guys in scoring position.”
His first at-bat Monday came with Betts 90 feet from home plate. Roberts had swapped Hernández and slumping Will Smith in the batting order, moving Hernández up to third and Smith down to fifth.
“For Teo to get three cracks at this guy, I like it,” Roberts said.
Right away, Hernández delivered. He fell into an 0-and-2 count but prolonged the at-bat and drove a fastball into right-center for a sacrifice fly.
The Brewers, however, evened the score without delay. Yamamoto struck out Jackson Chourio — whose leadoff home run last year was the lone run in Yamamoto’s NLCS complete game — to open the frame.
Then Brice Turang worked a full count and hit an opposite-field double. And William Contreras fought off a low slider, poking it into shallow left field to tie the score.
Two innings later, the Dodgers took the lead again, rewarded for hard contact as the Brewers’ defense showed its first signs of sloppy play. Tommy Edman led off with a single, and then Betts scorched a 100.9-mph one-hopper at shortstop Cooper Pratt, who mishandled it, giving Betts a single to put two runners on. Edman then advanced to third on a fly ball by Freeman.
Henderson tried to pick off Edman, but his errant throw gave the Dodgers the lead.
It didn’t last long.
In the bottom of the third, Yamamoto gave up a leadoff single and issued two walks before Yelich came up with two outs and drove a curveball into center field for two runs.
The first walk, to Turang, included a borderline ball four call. And the second, to Jake Bauers, came after 12 pitches.
As soon as Yamamoto left the game, it was clear it would be an uphill battle for the Dodgers.
The Dodgers retook the lead in the fifth with more help from the Brewers. After Kyle Tucker’s leadoff double, Edman laid down a sacrifice bunt. Henderson picked up the ball and sailed a throw to first, enabling the tying run to score.
Later in the inning, after former Dodger Dustin May replaced Henderson, Freeman hit a sacrifice fly, and Edman scored the go-ahead run.
This is postseason baseball, where the best pitchers take center stage and runs are at a premium. Would a stolen base or a sacrifice bunt every so often kill the Dodgers?
But, as had been the pattern all game, that 4-3 lead didn’t hold for long.
Roberts brought in left-hander Kris Bubic, replacing right-hander Roki Sasaki after a hitless inning, to face the left-handed-heavy heart of the order. But Bubic missed down the middle to the right-handed-hitting Contreras, who gave the fastball a ride over the center field wall, tying the score.
In the sixth, against Dodgers right-hander Brock Stewart, Contreras singled in the go-ahead run in a traffic-filled inning that included a Freeman error on a muffed pickoff attempt. Dodgers left-hander Tanner Scott came to the rescue and struck out Bauers and Yelich to end the inning, and Garrett Mitchell to kick off the seventh.
The Brewers added insurance runs in the eighth inning on RBI singles by Turang off hard-throwing right-hander Edgardo Henriquez and Bauers against left-hander Justin Wrobleski.

MILWAUKEE — Billboards around town promote the Milwaukee Brewers with the slogan “Win Our Way.”
The Dodgers tried. It didn’t work.
They scored four runs without getting a hit with a runner in scoring position – or hitting a home run. But the Brewers outhit them 12-3 and the final 15 Dodgers batters were retired in order as the Brewers pulled away to a 7-4 victory on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.
“They pitched well and they hit good,” Freddie Freeman said. “That’s the name of the game, and they did it better than us today.”
They did it twice in Milwaukee. The best-of-seven series now heads back to Los Angeles with the Dodgers trailing 2-0. Game 3 is Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Blake Snell scheduled to start for the Dodgers.
“Grind. Win one game at a time, one pitch at a time,” Mookie Betts said. “The mindset can’t really change. We can’t add more pressure. There’s already enough as it is. Keep it simple. One pitch at a time. Figure out a way to get a hit.”
They have played hard to get for the Dodgers this postseason. Through six games against the Atlanta Braves and Brewers, they are batting .193 (37 for 192) as a team and, most costly, 2 for 26 (.077) with runners in scoring position.
“I don’t have an answer why,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I know that they’ve got good arms. So do we. I think they’re just finding ways to win pitches better than we are. Sometimes you’ve got to find a way to get a base hit and those guys — there’s a lot of balls that weren’t hit hard tonight but found the outfield grass. That’s hitting.”
The Dodgers found ways to score without hitting early in Game 2.
The pesky, opportunistic Dodgers scored a run in the first inning without a hit. Betts drew a leadoff walk, moved to second on Freddie Freeman’s slow roller then third on a wild pitch and scored on a sacrifice fly by Teoscar Hernandez.
They scored again on a pair of singles and a wild pickoff throw by Brewers starting pitcher Logan Henderson who was more effective throwing home than he was to first base.
That came up again in the fifth inning. Kyle Tucker led off with a double and Tommy Edman tried to bunt him to third – you wanted bunts. Henderson did him one better, fielding the ball and throwing wildly to first base. Tucker scored on Henderson’s second error and Edman wound up scoring on a close play at the plate (confirmed by replay) on a sacrifice fly by Freeman.
Each of the runs either gave the Dodgers the lead or tied the game as the two teams played in a phone booth, never straying more than a run apart.
That was true, in part, because Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto was not sharp. He threw 75 pitches to get just two outs into the third inning. The Brewers swung at 33 of those pitches and only missed four times.
“He wasn’t as precise as he normally is,” Dodgers catcher Will Smith said. “I thought they did a really good job, not expanding out of the zone, taking advantage, especially up the middle.”
Two key decisions by Smith could have changed things, though.
On a 2-and-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the first inning, Yamamoto seemed to hit the outside corner with a cutter for strike three – or he didn’t. That was the call by home plate umpire Chris Segal. It might have been overturned by ABS but Smith did not challenge.
Two pitches later, Turang doubled. William Contreras drove him in with a single.
“Yeah, I went back and looked,” Smith said of the questionable call. “I don’t know if it clipped it or whatever. It was kind of early in the game. We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just get him out there.
“The walk one was a bummer but I guess it happens. It’s baseball.”
That came two innings later. The Brewers had a runner at second with one out when Yamamoto again appeared to hit the outside corner with a splitter on a full count to Turang. Segal called it a ball and Yamamoto appeared to gesture towards Smith that he wanted to challenge. Smith didn’t.
“That one was a splitter. It actually cut back a little bit,” Smith said. “I just saw it out (of the strike zone) and didn’t know if it came back enough or not.”
Two batters later, Jake Bauers won a 12-pitch battle with Yamamoto – the longest plate appearance against Yamamoto this season – fouling off six consecutive pitches before drawing a walk to load the bases.
“I was trying to work on the edge of the zone,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter. “And some pitches it was really good but he just stayed on it. He did a good job.”
Two pitches later, Christian Yelich stroked a two-run single through the middle, the first base hit off of a Yamamoto curveball since August 27 and the last pitch Yamamoto would throw in the game.
“That changed the game,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said of Bauers’ walk, adding that he was told the confrontation lasted seven minutes. “You think about that and what it does to a pitcher. He can get through an inning in less than seven minutes and he does all the time. He’s one of the best pitchers in the land. It was a great at-bat. I think a turning point, I really do.”
It started the Dodgers’ bullpen turning.
Roberts turned to Alex Vesia to finish off the third and gave the ball to Roki Sasaki for a scoreless fourth.
But then he took it away from the converted starter after just one inning and gave it to Kris Bubic with two lefties coming up in the fifth. In between them was Contreras and he tied the game with a solo home run off Bubic. The Dodgers never regained a lead.
“For me, I felt Bubic had 4 out of 5 left-handed hitters (coming up), and that’s a perfect spot for him,” Roberts said. “I knew they weren’t going to hit for them. You have Roki for an inning, and then you still have a guy — in my opinion, you’ve got a great spot for Bubic.
“That’s a decision I made, and we just didn’t — again, that’s his lane to be able to go out there and throw up a zero.”
The Brewers finally did things their way in the sixth inning against Brock Stewart.
He hit No. 9 hitter David Hamilton with a pitch. Hamilton went to second when Freeman mishandled a pickoff throw from Stewart and third on a ground out by Jackson Chourio. After an intentional walk of Turang, Contreras collected his third RBI of the game with a single to left field.
They did it again in the eighth against Edgardo Henriquez. Hamilton led off with a single, stole second and went to third on a ground out. Turang drove him in with an RBI single, giving the Brewers the first two-run lead for either team in this series. When Bauers drove in another run with a single, it gave the Brewers their first three-run lead this postseason.
Left to their own devices, the Dodgers couldn’t create another scoring opportunity. The final 15 batters went down in order against Brewers relievers Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby.
“They all throw 100 (mph) from different angles,” Freeman said.
The five perfect innings in relief are a postseason record. In winning the first two games of the NLCS, the Brewers’ bullpen has pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings.
“They attack hitters. They throw strikes. They’ve got good stuff, They throw hard,” Teoscar Hernandez said. “We just got to do a better job.
“I mean, they threw, the last two days, the same pitchers beside the starters. So we know what we’re gonna get during the games. They trust those guys. So that’s the guys that we’re gonna get.”
The Dodgers do not face elimination yet. But they must win two out of three at home in order to avoid it.
“We’ve got to find a way to get hits. That’s really it,” Betts repeated.
“They’re a really good ballclub. Really good arms. They’re swinging it. They’re playing really well. We have to come and be ready to go. There’s no secrets. We’re playing the game the same way. We’ve just got to find a way to get those hits.”

Best laid plans went awry very early in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series, the sloppiest and wildest game of the Dodgers postseason to date. In a game with four lead changes and two ties, the Dodgers couldn’t get a big hit to save their life, while William Contreras had three different run-scoring hits in the Brewers’ 7-4 win at American Family Field on Monday afternoon in Milwaukee.
The Dodgers head home to Los Angeles down two games to none, with their largest series deficit since the 2023 NLDS.
Chaos to start
It took until the 23rd half-inning of the series for one of these teams to score more than once in a frame, but it wasn’t for lack of trying. Both Jacob Misiorowski and Tarik Skubal labored in big innings in Game 1, but limited the damage to just one run in the rallies.
After single runs for both teams in the first inning, Yoshinobu Yamamoto ran into trouble. David Hamilton singled and stole second base. Brice Turang, who battled back from an 0-2 count and an unchallenged potential third-strike ball call for a double to score in the first inning, worked his way back from an 0-2 count again to walk in the third.
With two outs and two on, first baseman Jake Bauers fouled off six full-count pitches before earning a walk to load the bases.
“Yamamoto — it’s such a big pitch mix,” Bauers said during his media availability before the game. “There’s a lot that you have to try and deal with, and I think you can fall into the trap of trying to guess along with him.”
It took only two more pitches for Yamamoto to hang a curveball to Christian Yelich — in easily the worst of his 14 major league seasons — who singled home two to turn a Dodgers lead into a Dodgers deficit. It also ended Yamamoto’s day, stunningly after needing 75 pitches to get only eight outs, the shortest of his 11 postseason start with the Dodgers.
The dozen pitches to Bauers were the most in any single plate appearance in Yamamoto’s three years in the majors, the entire battle taking seven minutes, 15 seconds per the Fox broadcast.
Only way the Dodgers scored
Brewers starter Logan Henderson allowed only three hits, one of them a ball booted by shortstop Cooper Pratt. Henderson also walked two, but it was three errant throws that proved his undoing. His wild pitch in the first inning put Mookie Betts on third base directly before scoring on a sacrifice fly.
Henderson in the third inning with runners on the corners threw wildly on a pickoff attempt of Betts at first base, allowing Tommy Edman to score from third base. After Kyle Tucker doubled to lead off the fifth inning, Henderson had another throwing error when Edman tried to sacrifice, not only scoring Tucker but putting Edman on second base. He would later score on another sacrifice fly, on a play so close at the plate it required replay review to confirm.
Getting the big hits, or not
Contreras, the Brewers three-time All-Star catcher, singled home a run off Yamamoto in the first inning to tie the game, homered off left-hander Kris Bubic in the fifth inning to tie the game, then singled home a run off Brock Stewart in the sixth to give the Brewers the lead.
It was the third multi-hit game in these playoffs for Contreras, who has three home runs this October.
The Dodgers’ three-time All-Star catcher, Will Smith, was dropped to fifth in the batting order on Monday and was hitless in four at-bats. Smith has one single in 23 at-bats this postseason, with eight strikeouts.
“Obviously want the results to be a little better, but at the end of the day, it’s [six] games at the plate,” Smith told reporters in Milwaukee on Monday before Game 2. “No panic from me. So I’ll be fine.”
Smith isn’t alone in struggles at the plate.
Shohei Ohtani, still batting fourth, was hitless in four at-bats with two strikeouts in Game 2, and has three singles in 19 at-bats plus three walks this postseason.
The Brewers tacked on insurance runs in the eighth inning off Edgardo Henriquez and Justin Wrobleski with three singles and a walk. That put the Brewers up 7-4, the first time either team led by more than one run in this series.
Game 2 of the NLCS was just the second of 27 games this postseason in which both teams scored at least four runs.
Against Henderson the Dodgers were hitless in all of four total at-bats with runners in scoring position, dropping them to 2-for-26 with runners in scoring position this postseason. But once he left with no outs in the fifth inning, the Brewers bullpen completely shut things down the rest of the way.
Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby faced 15 batters and retired them all. Ashby pitched in multiple innings for a second straight day, this time earning the save.
The Dodgers now face a major uphill battle once they get back home.
NLCS Game 2 particulars
Home run: William Contreras (3)
WP — JoJo Romero (1-1): 1 IP 2 strikeouts
LP — Brock Stewart (0-1): 2/3 IP, 2 hits, 1 run, 1 walk, 1 strikeout
Sv — Aaron Ashby (1): 1 2/3 IP, 2 strikeouts
Up next
The NLCS moves location to Los Angeles beginning with Game 3 on Wednesday evening (5 p.m., FS1). Blake Snell probably starts for the Dodgers, though Dave Roberts earlier Monday wasn’t willing to confirm their plans just yet. Left-hander Robert Gasser starts on the mound for the Brewers.

MILWAUKEE –– The Dodgers were hoping to hit the reset switch on Monday.
Instead, all they did was slam down on the panic button.
Losing Game 1 of this National League Championship Series rematch against the Milwaukee Brewers was one thing. Dropping Game 2 on Monday, however, threatened to put their season in suddenly dire straits.
This time, after all, they weren’t facing a presumptive Cy Young Award winner like Jacob Misiorowski. This time, more importantly, they had their own postseason stalwart, reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, on the hill to calm the waters.
But in a 7-4 defeat at American Family Field, an unexpected thing happened.
Yamamoto, despite entering with a five-game playoff win streak and the second-lowest postseason ERA in the last 100 years, couldn’t steady the two-time defending champions.
The Brewers, who allowed Yamamoto to throw a complete game against them on the very same mound in Game 2 of last year’s NLCS sweep, turned the tables decisively with long, relentless, unforgiving offensive rallies.
“They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top to bottom, and then they put the ball in play, created havoc,” manager Dave Roberts said. “That’s what they do, and we didn’t do that. That’s the difference in the game … They did what needed to do tonight.”
Indeed, Yamamoto would last only 2 ⅔ innings in a 75-pitch grind against Milwaukee’s pesky, opportunistic offense. Despite being handed a pair of early one-run leads, he would depart the mound with the Dodgers behind.
It was a demoralizing turn of events –– keyed by a couple missed ABS challenge opportunities for Will Smith, an epic 12-pitch battle by Brewers slugger Jake Bauers, and a go-ahead two-run single from former MVP Christian Yelich that ultimately chased Yamamoto from the game.
While the contest would go back-and-forth from there, Yamamoto’s early exit gave the Dodgers’ bullpen too tall a task to withstand, sending the team back to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday desperately needing a response to a stunning two-games-to-none deficit.
“We got a lot of experience, we’ve been through everything before,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said. “So we’ll regroup tomorrow and go get ’em on Wednesday.”
The Dodgers did open the scoring Monday, manufacturing a first-inning run after Mookie Betts drew a leadoff walk, took second on a grounder, advanced to third on a wild pitch, then scored on a Teoscar Hernández sacrifice fly.
However, the Brewers responded with a rally of their own in the bottom of the first –– one that set the tone for their plan of attack against Yamamoto on Sunday.
With one out in the inning, Yamamoto seemed to freeze Brice Turang for a called third strike. But, home plate umpire Chris Segal inaccurately ruled it a ball, and Smith declined to use an ABS challenge behind the plate. Three pitches later, it would prove costly, with Turang getting a full-count fastball in the zone and slicing into left for a double. In the next at-bat, William Contreras came up and somehow stayed on a 2-2 slider less than a foot off the dirt, lofting a line drive just over Max Muncy’s head at third for an RBI single.
“It was kind of early in the game,” Smith said of the ABS decision. “We kind of had him on the ropes where we could just [try to] get him out there [even without the challenge].”
A similar story would play out in the third, as the Brewers erased a 2-1 lead the Dodgers took on an errant pickoff throw from Brewers starter Logan Henderson in the top half of the frame.
That inning began with a David Hamilton single. Then, after he stole second, Turang would again benefit from a missed ABS challenge opportunity –– with Smith declining to appeal another potential third strike in a full count, even as Yamamoto seemingly suggested he do so by pointing at his head himself on the mound.
“In that spot, Will didn’t feel like it was a strike,” Roberts said, trying not to secong-guess his catcher. “But obviously if you look back, [if] that’s a called third strike … that changes the outing.”
Once again, it set a disaster in motion. With an extra out to get, Yamamoto failed to complete the inning.
Instead, Bauers stepped up with two outs and forced Yamamoto into the longest plate appearance of his MLB career, drawing a walk from a grueling dozen-pitch battle.
After working a full-count, Bauers fouled off the next seven pitches he saw, chopping balls off the plate, to the backstop, into the seats, and –– twice –– just out of the reach of Dodgers fielders in foul territory.
The seven-minute duel went on so long, the battery in Yamamoto’s PitchCom device died after his 11th pitch, causing a delay while he was brought a replacement from the dugout.
“It just got to a certain point where it was straight compete mode,” Bauers said. “A little bit of a blackout, just kind of in the flow a little bit competing.”
Finally, on pitch No. 12, Bauers took a curveball in the dirt, loading the bases.
In the next at-bat, a clearly fatigued Yamamoto hung a curveball to Yelich, who lined his two-run single to center to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead.
That would be the end of Yamamoto’s day, marking the shortest outing of his playoff career. It would also leave too many innings for the Dodgers’ bullpen to cover –– even after the team retook the lead with a two-run rally in the fifth that was keyed by another throwing error from Henderson.
In the bottom of the fifth, Contreras greeted left-hander Kris Bubic with a towering game-tying home run that clanged off the bottom of the center-field scoreboard.
In the sixth, it would be Contreras again to push the Brewers back in front, lining a first-pitch single to left against Brock Stewart –– who had made his own mess by hitting a batter and firing an errant pickoff throw to first –– that gave the Brewers’ star catcher his third RBI of the day.
This time, the Dodgers wouldn’t have an answer, nor be gifted another pathway back into the game.
Rather, for a second-straight night, they were completely shut down by the Brewers’ bullpen, going 15 up, 15 down without a single baserunner after Henderson’s exit to finish the game with just three hits.
The Brewers, meanwhile, tacked on two insurance runs in the eighth, removing any pretense of late-game drama before a jubilant sell-out crowd.
Now, the Dodgers face a two-game hole they would have never imagined. Alarm bells are ringing. Their season, and World Series three-peat hopes, are dangerously close to being dashed.

The Los Angeles Dodgers once again were the first team to score but they couldn’t hold a lead over the Milwaukee Brewers for a second consecutive night and now are facing a 2-0 deficit in the National League Championship Series.
Other years the Dodgers trailed 1-0 in an NLCS but still won the pennant were 1988, 2018 and 2020. Only in 2020 did they also lose Game 2, which was part of overcoming a 3-1 series deficit against the Atlanta Braves.
Brewers 7, Dodgers 4: key takeaways from NLCS Game 2
Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s short start
Yoshinobu Yamamoto took the mound a career 3-0 with a 1.23 ERA in his three starts following a Dodgers’ loss in the playoffs. He also had a streak of pitching at least six innings and allowing just one run or fewer in four consecutive postseason starts.
That was snapped as Yamamoto labored on Monday, completing just 2.2 innings and exiting with the Dodgers trailing 3-2. Yamamoto in particular had trouble putting batters away after getting to two strikes. One notable example was Jake Bauers fouling off six pitches in a row before earning a walk on the 12th pitch in the third inning.
Despite his uncharacteristic outing, Yamamoto became the third pitcher to start an LCS game in each of his first three seasons. He joined 1998-2001 Orlando Hernández (first four) and 1991-93 Juan Guzmán.
Missed ABS challenges
There were two instances where Will Smith or Yamamoto would have benefitted from initiating a challenge with the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) system, and in both cases it came back to cost the Dodgers.
The first instance came on a 2-2 pitch to Brice Turang in the bottom of the first inning. It was called a ball despite catching the corner of the zone, and Turang doubled three pitches later. William Contreras’ RBI single then tied the game.
Turang was also batting in the third inning on another pitch that went in his favor. Yamamoto did appear to tap the side of his head, but was not convicted in doing so nor did he touch the top of his cap like players are instructed to. The walk put two on and the Brewers later loaded the bases before Christian Yelich delivered a two-run single that chased Yamamoto from the game.
Logan Henderson gifts runs to Dodgers
The Brewers, even if somewhat improbably, improved to 12-0 in Logan Henderson’s career home starts. He contributed to the Dodgers to manufacturing some offense in the first inning with a wild pitch allowing Mookie Betts to move to third base.
Teoscar Hernández’s sacrifice fly gave L.A. their initial lead. In the third inning, back-to-back singles by Betts and Tommy Edman put two on with nobody out, and the Dodgers scored the tying run on Henderson’s errant pickoff throw to first base.
Henderson committed another run-scoring throwing error after fielding Edman’s sacrifice bunt attempt.
That marked the end of the road for the Brewers’ rookie at four-plus innings pitched and four runs (two earned) allowed.
William Contreras powers Brewers
Milwaukee was carried by Contreras leading all players with xx RBI. Building off his RBI single in the first inning, Contreras tied the game again in the fifth on a solo home run off Kris Bubic.
Then after an intentional walk put runners at the corners with one out in the sixth inning, Contreras pulled an RBI single into left field that gave the Brewers their decided lead.

The Milwaukee Brewers set the series tone on Sunday night with a narrow victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1 of the NLCS. Powered by excellent infield defense, which produced three ground-ball double plays, an incredible swing from Brice Turang that led to a game-tying home run off Tarik Skubal, and another dominant performance from their bullpen, Pat Murphy's squad built a key 1-0 series lead in their quest to knock off the reigning back-to-back World Series champs.
After Turang's game-tying solo shot in the fourth, the Brewers took the lead in the bottom of the fifth thanks to an RBI single from rookie right fielder Luis Lara. The Brewers maintained that narrow one-run lead through the final four innings of the series opener, but they certainly had opportunities to add on to their run total.
Milwaukee's best scoring opportunity came in the bottom of the eighth inning. Jackson Chourio led off the inning with a single to right field off right-handed reliever Evan Phillips. After the leadoff hit, Dodgers manager turned to southpaw Tanner Scott to face Brice Turang, who promptly laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance Chourio to second base, setting up an RBI opportunity for William Contreras.
However, with the left-handed Scott on the mound, Roberts elected to intentionally walk Contreras, setting up a tough left-on-left matchup for Jake Bauers. Scott struck out Bauers on six pitches, which brought lefty-crusher Andrew Vaughn to the plate. Once again, Roberts elected to intentionally walk the righty to set up a left-on-left matchup with Garrett Mitchell. In doing so, however, Roberts moved a key insurance run to third base, where a passed ball or wild pitch would have given the Brewers a two-run lead, and a single would have given them a three-run advantage.
It was undoubtedly a risk for Roberts and the Dodgers -- loading the bases for Mitchell -- but one that paid off on Sunday night. However, in doing so, Roberts exposed a strategy he may use throughout the remainder of the series: prioritizing matchups between his left-handed relievers and the Brewers' left-handed hitters. Such a strategy means the Brewers lefties will have to find ways to produce against Los Angeles' tough bullpen southpaws throughout the series.
The pressure is on the Brewers' left-handed hitters to produce against Dodgers' tough lefty relievers
Left-on-left matchups are something the Brewers are bound to see a lot of throughout the NLCS. From starters Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell to a quartet of lefty relievers in Alex Vesia, Tanner Scott, Kris Bubic, and Justin Wrobleski, Milwaukee can expect to see plenty of southpaws throughout their rematch with the Dodgers.
Clearly, based on last night's strategy, Roberts is going to prioritize matching those lefties up with the Brewers' left-handed hitters by any means necessary. That means there will likely be situations, like last night, where Bauers, Mitchell, Brice Turang, and Christian Yelich will be asked to produce against a same-side pitcher. Concerningly for the Brewers, of that group only Bauers (.901 OPS vs. LHP) had an OPS better than .668 against left-handed pitching during the regular season.
Bauers commented on his improved success against left-handed pitching this year during his pre-game press conference on Monday morning, saying, "A lot of it just has to do with getting the opportunity to see them more often, and then I think I've really focused on developing an approach that gives me the best chance."
On the topic of opportunities, Bauers set a new career-high with 160 plate appearances against left-handed pitchers this year, and already that practice against lefties is coming in handy in the NLCS. Bauers acknowledged the difficult southpaws on the Dodgers' NLCS roster, saying, "Some of these guys, obviously it's not easy, whether it be high arm slot coming from behind you or someone throwing from the side," but in four at-bats in Game 1 last night, all of which came against left-handed pitchers, Bauers went 1-for-3 with a walk and a hard-hit single. Pair that with Turang's impressive blast off Skubal, and the Brewers' left-handers are off to a strong start against same-side pitchers in the NLCS.
Assuming Roberts continues to prioritize these matchups, even if it means intentionally putting runners on base, the pressure will be on Bauers, Turang, and the rest of the Brewers' lefties to continue putting together strong at-bats in these situations. If they can find success against southpaws early in the series, it will certainly complicate Roberts' pitching plan going forward.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Atlanta Braves, 3-2, on Sunday as the National League Division Series evened out to one game apiece. With the best-of-five series now heading back to Atlanta, the two-time defending champions are in a much more troublesome spot than expected.
Left-hander Blake Snell was far from his best on Sunday as he struck out five across 3.2 innings of work (90 pitches) with an earned run and five walks. Snell, Kris Bubic and Edgardo Henriquez all allowed an earned run while the four remaining relievers were hitless in their respective outings.
Offensively, Freddie Freeman tied things up in the fourth inning with a solo home run, just his second since the All-Star break. When the Dodgers were down to their final out, Max Muncy slugged a solo home run — but it was too little too late for LA.
The Dodgers also officially announced that the starter for Game 3 of the NLDS will be the ace: Right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. The reigning World Series MVP had a 2.16 ERA in his last five regular season starts and will now make his 2026 postseason debut.
Yamamoto will face off against southpaw Chris Sale for the Braves, who is working with a 2.16 ERA across 27 starts this season. So far in the postseason, Sale struck out nine across 6.1 innings in Atlanta's first wild-card game, and on one day of rest, closed out Game 3 of the wild-card round with three strikeouts across the game's final four outs.
Finally, manager Dave Roberts made a bold prediction regarding right fielder Kyle Tucker following his abysmal regular season to kick off the Dodgers chapter of his career. Tucker was hitting just .228 with 11 home runs going into September before he appeared to start to turn things around
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence," Roberts said before the NLDS. "You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and [I] expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—Tomorrow marks the start of the Los Angeles Dodgers’ quest for a third consecutive World Series championship, beginning with a rematch against the Atlanta Braves in the 2026 National League Division Series.
Today, both clubs hold their final workout before Saturday’s scorching mid-day opener, and we’ve got plenty of new updates and clarity on the Dodgers’ plans for the two games this weekend.
Dodgers’ NLDS Rotation Comes Into Focus With Skubal Tabbed for Game One
Leading up to the postseason, many asked what order the Dodgers would put on their star-studded starting rotation, and now we have part of an answer: two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal will start Game One of the NLDS against the Braves on Saturday.
That was a shock to many, especially since 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto was considered the clear-cut favorite to lead the charge in the postseason.
The move also isn’t entirely based on the Braves’ struggles versus left-handed pitching this season; Skubal on Friday confirmed that he learned of his Game One start way back during his last outing in San Francisco, where he tossed seven shutout innings to close his 2026 regular season.
While Dave Roberts was less revealing about his outlook for Games Two and Three of the NLDS, he admitted the team would have a decision by the end of Friday’s workout, but the stars are starting to align themselves on what the likely order will be.
Yamamoto, who faced hitters on Wednesday, is now lined up to start on regular rest against the Braves during Game Three, as reported by Taro Abe of Japan’s Chunichi Sports.
That would place left-hander Blake Snell for Game Two, after Skubal and before Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow, who threw a simulated game on Thursday for a possible Game Four if needed.
There were really no “wrong” answers for Dave Roberts and the Dodgers, but this allows them to focus on the Braves’ left-handed disadvantage and decide whether to go for the series sweep or swing with their best starter, Yamamoto, on the mound in Game Three, where he’ll likely go toe-to-toe with Chris Sale.
Dodgers Look to Exploit Braves’ Left-Handed Weakness With Southpaw-Heavy Staff
After tabbed left-hander Tarik Skubal with the ball in Game One of the NLDS, it starts a running theme for the Dodgers’ plan against the Braves, and that is their inability and struggles to hit left-handed pitching.
The Braves posted just a 91 wRC+ against southpaws during the regular season, tied for 24th in MLB. They also ranked 21st in wOBA (.306), 28th in OBP (.300), and tied for 16th in batting average (.240), while their 7.0% walk rate against lefties ranked 29th.
That combination gives the Dodgers plenty of reason to load up on southpaws in the NLDS, particularly with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell available. Skubal is already set to start Game One, giving Los Angeles a lefty right out of the gate.
Atlanta’s overall offense was productive enough to win 94 games, but its struggles against lefties provide the Dodgers with a specific weakness to attack throughout the series.
While the Dodgers have yet to announce a Game Two starter, all signs point to fellow left-hander Blake Snell, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto to follow him in Game Three at Atlanta.
As far as the Dodgers’ bullpen construction, depending on what split they have on the 26-man roster, they have plenty of left-handed options to choose from, including deadline acquisition Kris Bubic.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed Friday that the team would go with a 14-12 split for their 26-man roster, and with four starting pitchers, that leaves eight spots for the bullpen, with left-handers Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer and Alex Vesia locked for that role.
Chris Sale Likely Out of Games One and Two as Dodgers Avoid Atlanta’s Ace Early
In an effort to push the Braves past the Phillies for their first postseason series win since the 2021 season, Chris Sale came in on two days of rest out of the bullpen to collect the final four outs of Game Three.
Despite the Braves leading 6-2 and their closer, Raisel Iglesias, available in the bullpen, new Braves skipper Walt Weiss opted for the kill shot by bringing in his best pitcher, Chris Sale.
That move, however important it was for that particular game, has changed the landscape of the Braves’ pitching plan for the NLDS, as Sale is not lined up to pitch Game One and now may not be in play for Game Two on Sunday either.
“We’re gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it’s even close… A lot of it’s going to depend on how Chris feels… Certainly don’t want to jeopardize him and his health. He just happened to feel great yesterday when he got to the park, and that’s why he was in play.”
While this could simply be Walt Weiss playing a little October gamesmanship, keeping Chris Sale away from Games One and Two would certainly give Atlanta a chance to catch the Dodgers off guard, though Dave Roberts has plenty of postseason experience himself.
Of course, Weiss could also be telling the truth. If Atlanta really plans to save Sale for his return to Truist Park, the Braves’ decision to use him in relief during Game Three of the Wild Card Series becomes even more curious.
The Braves are already down two starters in left-hander Martín Pérez and right-hander Bryce Elder, with Weiss confirming that both will not be on the NLDS roster but possibly on the NLCS roster if Atlanta advances.
That leaves the Braves with a trio of Chris Sale (down until Game Three), Tyler Mahle, and Grant Holmes, who has been used in relief as a bulk inning guy from the bullpen.
The Braves are likely to launch a bullpen game for Game One in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Mahle set to start Game Two on normal rest after a masterful outing tossing seven innings of one-run ball.
Still, the likelihood of the Dodgers seeing Sale only once this series, and as late as Game Three, is a massive advantage for Dave Roberts and Co.
Dodgers vs. Braves: How the 2026 Head-to-Head Series Shook Out
The Dodgers didn’t exactly dominate their head-to-head matchup with the Braves this season. Los Angeles went just 1-5 against Atlanta in six regular-season meetings, getting outscored 26-15 in the process.
The teams first met at Dodger Stadium from May 8th-10th, with the Dodgers taking the opener 3-1 before Atlanta won the next two games by identical 7-2 scores. The Braves then delivered an even bigger blow in the final regular-season series, sweeping Los Angeles at Truist Park from August 25th-27th. Atlanta won the opener by one run, walked off in the middle game, and finished the sweep with a 1-0 Chris Sale shutout.
This matchup also comes with some unfinished postseason business. The Dodgers and Braves last met in the 2021 NLCS, when Atlanta knocked Los Angeles out in six games before winning the World Series. The Dodgers battled back from a 2-0 series deficit to cut the deficit to one game, but the Braves slammed the door in Game Six at Truist Park.
Five years later, the two teams meet again with another trip to the NLCS on the line. After Atlanta owned the regular-season matchup, the Dodgers now have a chance to change the story when the NLDS opens Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
